## Definition

The Acoustic Voice Quality Index (AVQI) is an objective method to quantify the
severity of overall voice quality in concatenated continuous speech and
sustained phonation segments [@barsties2016avqi]. It is a multivariate
construct based on linear regression that combines six acoustic markers into a
single score for the whole voice sample [@barsties2016avqi]. That score
represents the overall voice quality — the hoarseness level — of the sample
[@delgado2018avqi].

The index was developed by @maryn2010avqi and was one of the first measures to
combine both speech types [@delgado2018avqi]. The rationale for the combination:
sustained vowels are easily elicited and less affected by articulation and
dialect, while continuous speech is more representative of a patient's daily
voice [@delgado2018avqi].

## Computation

### Speech material and concatenation

The subject sustains the vowel [a:] for longer than 3 seconds, and a 3-second
mid-vowel portion is selected. The subject also reads a phonetically balanced
text aloud at comfortable pitch and loudness. For AVQI version 03.01 in Dutch,
the continuous-speech part is trimmed to the first 34 syllables of the text,
the 3-second [a:] segment is appended, and the result is saved as a single
sound file [@barsties2016avqi]. Acoustic analysis is applied only to the voiced
segments of the continuous speech — extracted by an automated Praat detection
script — plus the appended vowel segment [@barsties2016avqi].

### Component measures

All six parameters are obtained in Praat from the concatenated signal
[@barsties2016avqi; @delgado2018avqi]:

| Parameter | Definition |
|---|---|
| Smoothed cepstral peak prominence (CPPS) | Distance between the first rahmonic's peak and the point of equal quefrency on the regression line through the smoothed cepstrum — see the [CPPS chapter](cpps.qmd) |
| Harmonics-to-noise ratio (HNR) | Base-10 logarithm of the ratio between periodic energy and noise energy, × 10 |
| Shimmer local (Shim) | Absolute mean difference between amplitudes of successive periods, divided by the average amplitude |
| Shimmer local dB (ShdB) | Base-10 logarithm of the difference between amplitudes of successive periods, × 20 |
| General slope of the spectrum (Slope) | Difference between the energy in 0–1000 Hz and in 1000–10000 Hz of the long-term average spectrum |
| Tilt of the spectral trendline (Tilt) | The same difference computed on the trendline through the long-term average spectrum |

: The six AVQI components [@barsties2016avqi]. {#tbl-avqi-components}

### Regression equation (version 03.01)

As printed by @barsties2016avqi:

$$
\text{AVQI}_{03.01} = \bigl(4.152 - 0.177\,\text{CPPS} - 0.006\,\text{HNR}
- 0.037\,\text{Shim} + 0.941\,\text{ShdB}
+ 0.01\,\text{Slope} + 0.093\,\text{Tilt}\bigr) \times 2.8902
$$

The published Praat script displays the resulting score on a 0–10 axis, marked
green below the Dutch threshold of 2.43 and red above it [@barsties2016avqi].

::: {.callout-warning}
The printed equation differs between validation papers: @barsties2016avqi print
the HNR coefficient as 0.006 and the Tilt coefficient as 0.093 (and their
appendix script uses the same values), while @delgado2018avqi print 0.0006 and
0.0993 citing the same source. Use the coefficients from the official Praat
script rather than retyping them from any paper.
:::

### Versions 02.02 and 03.01

In the earlier AVQI versions the analyzed continuous-speech part was much
shorter than the constant 3-second vowel part (1.53 s of voiced speech in
Dutch, 1.99 s in Japanese) [@delgado2018avqi]. Version 03.01 balances the
analyzed durations of the two speech types by expanding the continuous-speech
sample from 17–22 syllables to around 34 syllables, for higher ecological
validity and balanced internal consistency [@barsties2016avqi;
@delgado2018avqi]. Early AVQI workflows required both SpeechTool and Praat;
once CPPS was implemented in Praat, the index ran in Praat alone, with highly
comparable outcomes [@barsties2016avqi].

The regression-based combination of measures over a concatenated sample was
explored for tracheoesophageal (alaryngeal) voice by @maryn2009cepstral, where
a two-factor model combining CPP with the prominence of the second spectral
harmonic reached *r~s~* = 0.87 with listener judgments.

## What it captures

The AVQI quantifies overall voice quality as judged by the grade (G) of the
GRBAS scale — the degree of hoarseness or voice abnormality [@barsties2016avqi;
@delgado2018avqi]. Concurrent validity with mean perceptual G is strong:
*r* = 0.815 in the Dutch external validation (66.4% of variance)
[@barsties2016avqi] and *r* = 0.835 in Spanish (69.7% of variance)
[@delgado2018avqi]. CPPS is the main factor in the multivariate model
[@barsties2016avqi]; meta-analytic evidence independently confirms cepstral
peak measures as among the most accurate acoustic measures of overall
dysphonia severity [@barsties2018meta].

Earlier AVQI investigations reported high sensitivity to voice changes through
therapy, supporting its use as a treatment outcome measure [@barsties2016avqi].

## Normative data

Diagnostic thresholds separate normophonic from hoarse voices, with hoarseness
defined as mean perceptual grade G ≥ 0.5 [@barsties2016avqi]:

| Population / language | Threshold | Sensitivity | Specificity | AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dutch, internal validation (60 samples, as reported) | 2.43 | 0.936 | 1.00 | 0.98 |
| Dutch, external validation (1058 samples) | 2.43 | 0.785 | 0.932 | 0.923 |
| Spanish (136 dysphonic, 47 normal) | 2.28 | 0.748 | 0.946 | 0.905 |
| Japanese (as reported) | 2.06 | 0.721 | 0.938 | 0.915 |

: AVQI 03.01 diagnostic thresholds [@barsties2016avqi; @delgado2018avqi]. {#tbl-avqi-thresholds}

Likelihood ratios at the optimal threshold: LR+ = 11.54, LR− = 0.23 (Dutch
external validation) [@barsties2016avqi]; LR+ = 13.85, LR− = 0.26 (Spanish,
threshold chosen by the Youden index) [@delgado2018avqi].

## Confounds and cautions

**Language-specific standardization is required.** The continuous-speech part
must be trimmed to a syllable count that yields about 3 seconds of voiced
speech, and the count differs by language: 34 syllables in Dutch, 33 in
Spanish, 30 in Japanese [@delgado2018avqi].

**Thresholds differ by language.** Reported optimal cutoffs are 2.43 (Dutch),
2.28 (Spanish), and 2.06 (Japanese). The differences are small — AVQI appears
relatively insulated from inter-language phonetic differences — but the
language-specific cutoff should be used [@delgado2018avqi].

**Recording conditions matter.** Validation recordings were made in sound-
treated rooms with head-mounted condenser microphones at 44.1 kHz / 16 bit,
with environmental noise verified against a signal-to-noise norm
[@barsties2016avqi; @delgado2018avqi]. The AVQI script itself states that
reliable analysis requires optimal data-acquisition conditions
[@barsties2016avqi].

**Report the version.** Versions 02.02 and 03.01 differ in the length of the
continuous-speech part and in the regression weighting; scores are not
comparable across versions [@barsties2016avqi].

**Base rates affect ROC statistics.** The Dutch external validation sample
contained 8% normophonia and 92% dysphonia; likelihood ratios were used
because they are less vulnerable to base-rate differences than ROC statistics
alone [@barsties2016avqi].

**Voicing detection is part of the pipeline.** Voiced segments are extracted
automatically before measurement, so results depend on that detection step
[@barsties2016avqi].

## Validation

Across 1118 subjects in two studies, AVQI 03.01 showed a homogeneous weighted
mean correlation of *r* = 0.821 with perceptual overall voice quality, against
*r* = 0.790 for the initial AVQI model pooled over 507 subjects
[@barsties2016avqi]. In the same pooled analysis, the Dysphonia Severity Index
reached a heterogeneous weighted mean *r* = 0.524 and the Cepstral Spectral
Index of Dysphonia *r* = 0.788 (sustained vowel) and 0.748 (continuous
speech); AVQI 03.01 reached the highest concurrent validity among these
multiparametric indices [@barsties2016avqi]. Language validations include
Dutch [@barsties2016avqi] and Spanish [@delgado2018avqi], with Japanese
figures reported in the latter.
